name: MCP3301-CI_SN
title: MCP3301: 13-bit low-power ADC with a differential input and an SPI port
summary: A single-channel successive-approximation ADC that converts the difference between two inputs to 12 bits plus sign, in two's complement, at up to 100 ksps from a 4.5 V to 5.5 V supply. An external reference of 400 mV to VDD sets the span of ±VREF. The result is read over a three-wire SPI port in 16 clocks; between conversions the part idles at typically 50 nA. Two linearity grades, B (±1 LSB INL) and C (±2 LSB INL), come in 8-pin MSOP, PDIP and SOIC; MCP3301-CI/SN is the C grade in SOIC.
key_figures: 100 ksps max at VDD = 5 V (FCLK = 1.7 MHz)
±1 LSB max (B grade), ±2 LSB max (C grade)
±1 LSB max, no missing codes over temperature
4.5 V to 5.5 V specified; operates from 2.7 V
300 µA typ, 450 µA max at 5 V; standby 0.05 µA typ, 1 µA max
0.4 V to VDD; 100 µA typ, 150 µA max
SINAD 78 dB, THD -91 dB, SFDR 92 dB typ

notes: The order code is MCP3301, grade letter, temperature letter, then /package. MCP3301T in place of MCP3301 is the same part on tape and reel.
MCP3301-CI/SN is the C-grade industrial part in 150 mil SOIC.

pins.name: VREF
pins.function: Reference voltage input. Sets the full-scale input span and the LSB size; any instability of the reference source shows directly in the conversion result.

pins.name: IN(+)
pins.function: Positive analog input. Absolute range VSS - 0.3 V to VDD + 0.3 V; full scale is the magnitude of IN(+) - IN(-).

pins.name: IN(-)
pins.function: Negative analog input. Absolute range VSS - 0.3 V to VDD + 0.3 V.

pins.name: VSS
pins.function: Ground. Tie to the analog ground plane where the board has one.

pins.name: CS/SHDN
pins.function: Chip select, active low; driving it low starts communication. Driving it high ends a conversion and puts the part in low-power standby. It must go high between conversions and cannot be held low across several.

pins.name: DOUT
pins.function: SPI serial data output. Shifts out the conversion result; changes on each falling clock edge. High impedance while CS/SHDN is high.

pins.name: CLK
pins.function: SPI serial clock. Starts the sample and clocks out each result bit as it is converted; its speed is bounded by the source impedance and by the 85 kHz minimum during conversion.

pins.name: VDD
pins.function: Supply, +4.5 V to 5.5 V for specified performance (the part runs from 2.7 V). A 0.1 µF ceramic bypass capacitor goes as close to this pin as possible.

circuits.title: Load circuit for tDIS and tEN

Tied to VDD it gives tDIS waveform 2 (output otherwise low), to VDD/2 the tEN waveform, and to VSS tDIS waveform 1 (output otherwise high). tDIS runs from CS/SHDN crossing VIH to DOUT reaching 90 % (waveform 1) or 10 % (waveform 2).

circuits.title: Power supply sensitivity test circuit (PSRR)
circuits.description: Half of an MCP602 op amp, with 1 kΩ feedback and 1 kΩ to ground, takes a 2.63 V DC level through 1 kΩ and a 5 VP-P sine through 20 kΩ at its non-inverting input and delivers 5 V with ±500 mVP-P ripple to VDD of the converter under test.

parts.note: one half of the dual op amp
to VDD on the converter under test

notes: The op amp's supply pins are not shown.

circuits.title: Full differential test configuration
circuits.description: The configuration the electrical characteristics are measured in: two 5 VP-P sources in series drive IN(+) and IN(-), their junction held at a 2.5 V common-mode source. VREF = 5 V with 1 µF and 0.1 µF to ground; VDD = 5 V with 0.1 µF.

circuits.title: Pseudo differential test configuration
circuits.description: One 5 VP-P source drives IN(+) while IN(-) sits on a 2.5 V common-mode source. VREF = 2.5 V with 1 µF and 0.1 µF to ground; VDD = 5 V with 0.1 µF.

circuits.title: Pseudo-differential biasing circuit for bipolar operation
circuits.description: A single-ended signal is AC coupled through 10 µF into IN(+), and 1 kΩ biases IN(+) at the 2.5 V output of an MCP1525 reference, which also drives IN(-) and VREF. The output spans -4096 to +4095 with a 610 µV LSB. The 10 µF and 1 kΩ set a 100 Hz high-pass corner; a larger C lowers the corner, and R is kept at 1 kΩ or less because more source impedance needs more acquisition time.

circuits.title: Op amp gain stage and input buffer
circuits.description: An MCP6022 op amp, with 10 kΩ feedback and 1 kΩ to the 2.5 V node, adds gain and buffers the signal into IN(+), so the source may have a high impedance. The input is AC coupled through 1 µF and biased by 1 MΩ to the 2.5 V MCP1525 output, which also sets IN(-), VREF and the gain stage's reference point. The op amp output cannot reach the rails, so some of the input range is lost.
notes: The op amp's supply pins are not shown.

circuits.title: Gain stage with a 2.048 V reference below the 2.5 V bias
circuits.description: The gain stage of amp-gain built with an MCP606, with VREF moved to a 2.048 V shunt reference fed from VDD through 10 kΩ while the signal stays biased at the 2.5 V MCP1525 output. Holding VREF a little under the common-mode voltage keeps the full-scale span inside the op amp's output swing.
notes: The op amp's supply pins are not shown.

circuits.title: Second-order anti-aliasing filter driving the input
circuits.description: An MCP601 unity-gain follower forms a second-order 10 Hz Butterworth low-pass filter (7.86 kΩ and 14.6 kΩ in series, 2.2 µF fed back from the output, 1 µF to ground) and gives IN(+) a low-impedance drive; IN(-) is grounded. An MCP1541 supplies a 4.096 V reference with 1 µF load capacitance. VDD carries 10 µF and 0.1 µF at the converter, and 0.1 µF at the reference input.
notes: The op amp's supply pins are not shown.

operation.text: A successive-approximation converter with a sample-and-hold on both inputs. The voltage between IN+ and IN- is captured on the internal sample capacitors for 1.5 clock periods (tACQ); then the hold switches open and the stored charge is converted over 13 clock periods, one per bit, into a 13-bit two's complement result. The first bit out is the sign, which says whether IN+ or IN- is the higher input.

Communication starts when CS/SHDN falls. If the part powered up with CS/SHDN already low, CS/SHDN has to be taken high and low again first. Sampling begins on the first rising CLK edge after CS/SHDN falls and ends on the falling edge of the second clock, when DOUT drives a low null bit. The next 13 clocks shift out the result, sign bit first, then B11 down to B0; DOUT always changes on falling edges. If clocks continue with CS/SHDN low, the result is sent again LSB first (B1 up to B11 and the sign), and after that zeros for as long as clocks arrive. CS/SHDN must return high between conversions (tCSH).

Once the conversion is finished (tDATA), the bias current and the comparator shut down and VREF becomes a high-impedance node, while the clock can carry on reading out the reversed-order data and then zeros. Raising CS/SHDN ends the conversion and puts the part into standby, where it draws typically 50 nA.

A conversion takes 16 clocks, which is two 8-bit transfers. Because the part drives DOUT on falling edges, the controller latches on rising edges: SPI mode 0,0 (clock idles low) and mode 1,1 (clock idles high) both work. After the first byte the receive register holds two unknown bits (DOUT is high impedance for the first two clocks), the null bit, the sign bit and B11 to B8; the second byte holds B7 to B0.

The result is binary two's complement with a leading sign bit: 0 when IN+ is above IN-, 1 when IN- is above IN+. With IN+ equal to IN- both the sign and the data are zero. The code reaches +4095 when IN+ - IN- = VREF - 1 LSB and -4096 when IN+ - IN- = -VREF.

Full differential operation drives both IN(+) and IN(-) with signal (circuit full-diff-test). Pseudo-differential operation applies a single-ended signal to one input and biases the other above VSS, giving bipolar codes (circuit pseudo-diff-test). Bipolar operation uses all 8192 codes. Unipolar operation uses one side of the transfer function only, which amounts to a 12-bit converter.

Both inputs see the same model (table: Analog input model): the source impedance adds to the 1 kΩ sampling switch, and together they must charge the 25 pF sample capacitor to 13-bit accuracy within the 1.5-clock acquisition period. A low-impedance source can drive the pin directly. A higher source impedance with no more acquisition time raises the offset, gain and integral nonlinearity errors; a slower clock lengthens acquisition, and the curve of maximum clock frequency against source resistance gives the limit for ±1 LSB INL. Buffering with an op amp removes the impedance problem, and a low-pass filter ahead of the input keeps aliasing signals out of the result.

During conversion the held charge leaks away if the clock is slow, so the clock should run at 85 kHz or faster through tCONV; slower clocking can add linearity errors beyond the ratings. Apart from that, and provided every timing limit is met, there is no requirement on clock speed or duty cycle during the conversion cycle.

The common-mode voltage may be anywhere in the absolute input range, VSS - 0.3 V to VDD + 0.3 V, but using the full conversion range limits its swing for a given VREF; a smaller VREF leaves a wider common-mode window (table: Common-mode range against VREF). VREF down to 400 mV changes INL and DNL by less than 0.1 LSB.
In circuit bias-bipolar the converter is not production tested at VREF = 2.5 V; its linearity changes by no more than 0.1 LSB from the tested case.

An op amp output that cannot swing to the rails costs input range when the signal swings 0 V to 5 V. A VREF slightly below the common-mode voltage avoids it: a 2.048 V reference with the signal biased at 2.5 V (circuit amp-2v048-ref).

VREF may be set from 400 mV to 5 V (up to VDD). The reference draws typically 100 µA while converting and 0.001 µA with CS/SHDN high. When an external reference IC drives VREF, follow the layout guidance for that reference; instability of the reference shows up in the result.
The part operates from 2.7 V to 5.5 V; the specified performance applies from 4.5 V to 5.5 V. Typical operating current is 300 µA at 5 V; 450 µA is the maximum.

Bypass VDD to ground with 0.1 µF placed as near the pin as possible. Keep digital and analog traces well apart, run no traces under the device or its bypass capacitor, and route high-frequency lines such as the clock far from analog traces. An analog ground plane keeps every device at the same ground potential, and feeding VDD to each device from one point in a star cuts errors from shared return currents.

INL is the largest departure from a straight line through the end points of the bipolar transfer function, the end points lying 1/2 LSB above the first transition (0x1000) and 1/2 LSB below the last (0x0FFF). DNL is the difference between the measured step of two adjacent code transitions and the ideal 1 LSB. Positive gain error is the deviation of the last positive transition (0x0FFF) from VREF - 1/2 LSB, and negative gain error that of the last negative transition (0x1000) from -VREF - 1/2 LSB, each after removing the bipolar offset. Offset error is the deviation of the first positive transition (0x0001) from 1/2 LSB. SFDR is the fundamental's rms value over the next largest spectral component, usually the first harmonic but possibly a noise peak.
